blocks.x: First thing I want to do is get everybody's name down. What's your name? Edward Richardson. Mm-hmm.
Marjorie Zander.

Dick Allen. I see. Where were you born, Richardson? In New Orleans. What section? They call it the battlefield. That's over around Lafayette and Cypress. Lafayette and Cypress. Yeah. You know I forgot to put today's date on this thing and what are we doing on it? See we're recording in the library in Seminar Room 2, Tulane University. And what's today's date? October the, I can't think. 29th I believe. October the 29th, 1960. So you were born around Cypress and Lafayette, that's your neighborhood? That's right. That's right. Where is Cypress? I can't place it. Cypress, it's uh, was just about two blocks on the downtown side of the New Basin Canal. Oh yeah. See. And what's the exact date of your birth? 18th of April. What year? 1903. 1903. 1903. Yeah. I see. Did you listen to music much before you played? Well, I did. I listened to Rainey most of the time, Kid Rainey. And they had a brass band they called Excelsa. I used to love to listen to them play parades. Mm-hmm. I see. And uh, did anybody in your family play music around the home? No, no. I was the only one. Mm-hmm. They sang? No. No, no. I thought maybe you picked up some talent through them somehow. No, I just brushed that up my own self. Mm-hmm. I see. Uh, when you started listening to Rainey and Excelsa, do you remember any of the guys in those different bands? Well, no. I can't remember anybody but Rainey now. Mm-hmm. That's been so long, I couldn't remember. How old were you when you started listening to Rainey? Well, I was about 17 years old. And when did you start following parades? Well, I guess I was about around my 20s because in those times, when you're around about 16 and 17 years old, old people were so close on you, you couldn't get out around those things. Mm-hmm. So I was around my teens when I started following parades. You couldn't sneak off when you were young. No, no. It wouldn't have to be your parent. It would be somebody else that would know you and it would be just as bad as your parent. Mm-hmm. You remember the guys in the Excelsior at all at that time? No, I can't remember. You don't remember the leader? The leader of the Excelsior? No. See? Well, when did you first start playing yourself? Well, I can't exactly call the time, but I was real young. I guess I was about in my 20s. About in my 20s when I started playing. We had Professor Hansberry. He was learning us. You remember his full name? No, I can't remember his full name. You started off with a teacher or started off playing by yourself? No, I started off with a teacher, Hansberry. And how did he teach you? Well, he was all right. I think he was a nice person. And that means a plenty when you know how to treat young people. That most encourages him. Well, did he have a method or did he start you out with his own stuff? Well, he did have some of his own stuff, but he would write it out. Write in music, make his own parts out that he wanted you to play, to learn you on. And that's how I did the start. Do you remember any of the little tunes he started you out on? Well, I believe about the first piece we learned how to play was Little Lies of Jane. Yeah, that's a old one I'm a. Did you play as a group when you first started or would he give you lessons by yourself? Well, he gave lessons to each one of us, about a month or two. And then we tried to organize a little band. We had Albert Brown playing drum, Charlie Lonzo playing guitar. And I can't remember the rest. Charlie Lonzo, is he left handed or right handed guitar player? He was right handed. Yeah, I got him confused with another fellow. I know a left handed guitar player named Charlie and I can't ever find out his name. But that's something you don't see very often, you know. Left handed. No, you very seldom see that. I haven't seen him in years. He used to play around with Noon and Sam, I guess it was. Well, this Charlie, what I'm telling you about, he's gone now. He's passed. How long? Good while. Oh yeah, he's been gone about fifteen, sixteen years. Well, that wouldn't be the same fellow. Because that was recent. How big a band did you have when you were playing? Well, we had about seven pieces. We had seven pieces. Did you read all your stuff? Oh yeah. Most of what we did was reading. Yeah. Like Liza Jane and those kind of numbers, well, it was by head. About how many head numbers did you have in all? Well, I had about three, about four. Had Summer These Days, Down By The Riverside. That was a hymn. We used to play it in jazz. Tipperary, a long ways from Tipperary. That's about all I can remember. About that time, who were some of the other trumpet players you listened to aside, Renee? And you were just getting started. Well, Buddy P.T. He was one of the old trumpet players. And there was another trumpet player, he learned me a good bit. His name was Baptiste Brown from Martin Carlton. He learned me a good bit. I'd go sometime and get him up out of his bed. He'd be asleep. Sit on the side of his bed to learn me. Was he a good reader? Yes, he was good. And how did he teach you? Did he use a method? Well, yes. But I'd forgotten the name of the method he had. And then he'd write manuscripts for me. Did you say whether Hanbury had a method or not at all? Or did he write it all out? I'm not sure. I think he did have a method, a book of some sort, but I can't place a name of it. Well, back to the other trumpet players. Oh, I know what I wanted to ask you. Did Hanbury play in any bands himself? No, not as I know of. He was just an instructor at that time. And Bat Brown, what about him? He played with bands, didn't he? Bat... Bat... Bat... Bat... Batiste Brown? Oh, yeah. Batiste Brown used to play... I can't call the name of the band. Where did they play? Did they play steady in place? No, they mostly played parades. They mostly played parades. Well, when you got this little band organized, did you play any jobs for free or did you get money? Well, the most we did was we didn't sign any kind of contracts of any sort. We just would accept what was given. So it was mostly like free. Where did you play? Where did you play? Well... I'm trying to study. The last place I played was down on Claiborne Avenue. Claiborne and what? I forgot. It was on the back of town side of the bank. We used to play there every Sunday evening. About what neighborhood? No, I've forgotten. Uptown? Downtown. Down below Canal? Yeah, below Canal. It was about three blocks on the downtown side of Lision Field. Around Maroney in that neighborhood. Well, I wouldn't say exactly yes because I kind of confused those streets. Yeah. Well, anyway, did you get, how much would you get when they did pay you on the jobs like that, if you don't mind telling me when you're still? Well, we'd make sometimes three dollars, three or four dollars. Well, that's pretty good pay. And tips. That's three dollars in all or three dollars a man? Three dollars a man. Yeah. That's very good for those times. Okay. Then after that, what did you do? Well, by the way, whose band was that? I'm trying to, did they have any leader? Did you all just split it? Well, they mostly, no they didn't have a leader. It was George Jones' band. That early band? Yeah, George Jones. He was an old guitar player, sometime he'd play bass. Used to sing, comedian like. What would he sing? Old Lies of Jane was his favorite number. Do you have any funny songs other than that? No, I can't remember any other. Mm-hmm. Just those old numbers like Lies of Jane, Alabama Bomb, Long Waves from Tipperware, High Society, Tiger Rags. Mm-hmm. Let's see. Well, how long was that band up? Well, I couldn't exactly estimate the time. Mm-hmm. I was up about a year or two. Could have been about that long. Play any parades when you were? No. Not then. No. I didn't play any parades until I met Kid Rainey. Mm-hmm. Then he started taking me out on his jobs. Parade jobs? Parade jobs, uh-huh. Who would he have with his band? Well, Rainey would use, I can remember, George Lewis sometime, the clarinet player. Mm-hmm. And sometime Buddy P.T. That's the only three I can remember. Mm-hmm. Who would he have on snare drum? No, I can't remember his snare drum player. You don't remember drum, sir? No. If I'm not sure, I believe that was Rainey's brother, the drummer. Kid Rainey's brother. I guess it would be. Yeah. Uh, that reminds me, uh, you know who I saw up in the country a few months ago was, uh, Morris French. Morris French? Do you remember him, the trombone player? Yeah, it's been many years since I seen Morris, so I don't think I'd know Morris if I'd seen him. You know him. We took a ride up there with Punch, you know. Did you ever play with him? No, I never did play with him. Uh, what was your band after George Jones, after that first band? After George Jones? Well, I tried to organize an orchestra once, but we didn't have any success. I had, uh, a lady by the name Louise Delvar was my pianist. I had Duffy on sax. I had Albert Brown, a drummer. That's about all of them I can remember. I don't remember Duffy. Duffy was a saxophone player. First name, do you remember that? No. All I can remember is Duffy. Did he play alto or Ternal? Alto. So that didn't last very long, it didn't? No, we didn't make a success, no success whatsoever. So we just had to split up and get what we could. The piano player that I was playing with, Louise Delvar, she was the organist at St. Catherine's Church. Well, she just continued there. I guess that played pretty well, huh? Oh yeah. I mean, I pretty well. She was good. Was that a reading band? Oh yeah. Most of us had music. We had to read music. Just a few numbers, like people would want, like those numbers that I first called, they was by head. Old Lives of Jane and all those things. They was by head. Well, what happened after that band, do you remember? Well, after that band broke up, we didn't have anything to do and nobody was interested in organizing the band. We just played well, we could get a little job there. I think that's when I started playing a few jobs with René Perez, Kid René. Was that before depression or after? That was before depression. So you were pretty young. Oh yeah, yeah. So you started playing with René in the street. Did René's brass band read? Yeah. Oh yeah. They had music. And did you have any dance jobs with them? No, I never did play a dance job with René. How did that brass band sound with him and Buddy and you there? How would you work that out? Say the three trumpets. Well, I think it was real good. I'd play second lots of times, but I mostly preferred to lead. But by them being older musicians than me, they know it more than I know. Give them a preference, let them lead, and I'd be satisfied playing at second. Who would lead? René, Kid René. Would lead. Yeah. Well, if you had to take your choice, who would you say was better than Barrett's Buddy or René? Well, I think they're about, both of them are about the same. Buddy and René, they was, I couldn't tell what one was the best because both of them was real good trumpet players. Did you hear Louis Armstrong back in that time? I can't remember, Louis. I remember when I was a boy, the 34th of May, we'd go to Camp Chalmette. That was Armstrong Day. But I can't, he, Louis Armstrong would play for us, but I can't remember Louis. Were you playing then? Oh no, I was too young then. I was a boy then. Well, he must have been a boy too, huh? He was young because he, we'd, somehow or another, we'd get in contact with him from, from the boys' homes. That's where they'd get the band from. I think Shots was there with him too. I can't remember Shots in that time. No. No. I remember Shots seeing him around the, that story, he used to play music on that story. And the Copperators Hall, those old halls. You went to dances before you played? Oh yeah, yeah I did. Where did you? The Copperators Hall, the Economy Hall, the Roof Garden on top of the Epithian Temple a long time ago. And then we had different places would give what you call lawn parties. And it'd be in the neighborhood not too far, I'd go there. Who would be in those different halls? What you mean, the musicians? What bands? Yeah, what bands would be playing those different kinds of jobs around? Oh well they'd have sometime Shots, Rene, and that's about all. I can remember in those halls they'd have sometime, this fella from over the river, trumpet player, Sun Allen. He'd be over there in those halls sometime. Overline Allen's son? Yeah that's right. I've seen it have a contest, it'd have Celestan on one end of the hall and Sun Allen on the other side, other end. And those two bands would put on some music. Remember who won? Well no, they never would have a contest of that sort, not when I was there. They'd both have turns to play music and everybody just got along nice. Well, sometimes that's best, you know?
It is.

Everybody be agreeable. Just a second. We're talking about the dance halls and lawn parties and all that, you said you heard Sun Allen and Celestan. That's right. And what about lawn parties? Do you remember who played those? Well Buddy P.T. and Sam, they played those lawn parties. And there's another musician, I'm trying to call his name. No I can't think of his name now. A trumpet player too. Who was Sam? You said Sam played him. Sam Morgan. Yeah, that was a trumpet player too. That was Albert Morgan's brother. They'd play those lawn parties and those different things like that. Sam have a good band? Oh yeah. Yeah, Sam had a nice band. You know any of the fellas in there? No, I was too young, I just mostly knowed Sam. I was interested in the trumpet then and he was a trumpet player and somehow or another looked like that's all I'd mostly be after. Turn this off and turn it on high and lift it. Did any of the bands use two trumpets as dancers? Oh yeah. Celestan used to use two trumpets. Sam Morgan, he used two trumpets. Most all the bands used two trumpets at that time. Do you remember who Celestan's second trumpet was? Well the last second trumpet I noted was Sam Morgan you said? Yeah. No. Do you know who the trumpet with Celestan was, the other one? Was Albert, I can't think of his maiden name, Albert from Over the River. He played second trumpet with Celestan. No I'll figure it out. Yeah. Albert from Over the River. What did he look like? Well he was a light complected fellow. I think I've heard you call his name. That's not the guy that used to play violin that I showed you a picture. No. No he never did play violin. One of the trumpet players I know over there are Charlie Love and Peter Bocash that I can think of offhand, Old Man Allen and Sonny Allen. But you know it'll come to you in a little while. Yeah, yes. I was trying to think. But when you were playing with Renee in the brass band did you have a steady dance job or anything? No I never did play a dance with Renee. No but I mean were you working with anybody else? No. No. You were just playing brass band? That's all. Were you working during the day then? I mean at night? No. No I didn't have any other job. Just playing brass band music and making it that way? Well at that time I was rather young and I didn't have to look for my own support because my people mostly did that for me. Yeah. I'm trying to think of the other trumpet player that was Son Allen. Was Son Allen played second with Celestan? That's right. With Celestan.
Well about how often were you playing parades?

Well that was seldom. They didn't have as many parades as they have now. And just whenever Renee would get a parade well he'd use me to play with him. And that wouldn't be too often. That'd be some Sundays. Like different clubs would have a turn out. Well they'd use his band and I'd get a chance to play then. What clubs would they be? Remember any other names? Well it would be the Dewars Club. Sometimes the Tulane. That's all I, and there's another one, the Violet, Violet's Club. That's about all I can remember. Would they have big parades? Oh yeah they'd have nice parades. Just like you see the parades they have now. Different organizations turned out, they turned out the same way in those times. Would they dress up as much as the Dolly Bunch then? Oh yeah. Yeah they dressed. So it's fancier than it is now, huh? Well no, I wouldn't say it is. I wouldn't say it was more fancy in those times. Like times is going on, everything is brightening up, you know? So the Dolly had a little difference in it. Did they have horses in the parades there or no? No. I never remember any horses. Everybody would be walking. No cars? No, no cars. I guess they had cars in those days, that's right. They had cars but they didn't use them for that occasion, you know? Everybody looked like they enjoyed walking, stepping with the music. How many funerals would you play say during the course of a month then? Would Rene get many funerals? No, he didn't get many funerals. Funerals would sell him. We'd probably play about two or three funerals, about four funerals in a year's time. But he didn't do much.
Well when you weren't playing did you watch other bands in the streets?

Well sometime I would. I'd have time to. We'd watch the Tuxedas. And they had another band there. I believe it was the Excelsior. I can't exactly call the name of it. The most was then known was the Tuxedo. Tuxedo band and Rene's band. That was the two brass bands that they had for parades.
Did you all play pretty much the same numbers?

Well yes, yes. They mostly played alike. They played the same things. They'd have a few marches. And then those old hymns like By and By. That's when they'd have funerals. They'd take their body with hymns and on their way back, well they'd change that. They'd have to play songs for the second line to enjoy it. What would be some of the hymns and marches and songs and all that that you would play? Do you remember the names of any of them? Yeah, Over in the Glory Land. Sing On. I can't think of them right now. They played a good many hymns. Saints. They used that then, the Saints. That's about all I can remember.
Did you all read the hymns?

Well, we mostly played those hymns by head. Just by listening to it. Get the sound of it. I don't remember them having those hymns with music. I would get a chance to look at music, those books that they use in the choirs, in these churches, and that's how I did to catch it. And of course when I'd catch it there I'd go on with them and play it by head. What about the marches? You read them or play them by head? Well no, you had to read the marches. The march, I can remember we used to have the old march Maryland. Well they had music for that. It was rather complicated, you couldn't so well play that by head, by changing keys. Did you all play it like you did when you were with the Eureka? Oh yeah. It was about the same arrangement and everything. Yeah, the same music. Same arrangement. I see. Did Rene take that trumpet solo that Percy takes? Yeah. Oh yeah. He was good at that. Did he play it at the same range that Percy would, or would he play it high or low or what? I think they played just about the same. Rene and play some of it, they played about the same music. What about, go ahead. I was going to say, is that on some particular number you're talking about?
Maryland we're talking about. Oh. At least I was talking about Maryland.

Yeah, that's an old march Maryland. What about songs coming back in those days? What would you play coming back? For the second line? Oh like from a funeral? Mm-hmm. Well they played like the Sheik, Maury, put on your old gray bonnet. Yeah, those three numbers, I'd about hold them up. Old gray bonnet used to be a hit one time. When did the band start playing blues? Well those blues was mostly used in like dance halls. And when they'd get around about 10 o'clock, 11 o'clock, they'd start playing blues. They'd have a lot of jump numbers until around about that time. When they'd get late they'd play blues. When did they start playing blues in the street? Well if somebody would ask for a blues like that, those second lines, they'd get together and ask for a blues, they could play a blues in walk time. They'd play St. Louis blues and sometimes the old blues.

Well, what happened after you left René? Well, that's when I tried to organize my own band. I didn't have any luck. Oh, I see. So, uh, let me see now. Then after that, who did you join up with? Well, it was quite a while. They had a man by the name of Jimmy Jackson. Jackson had a band. And he got in touch with me whenever he'd get parade jobs, well he'd hire me, play with them. Jackson's band, Jimmy Jackson's band. And what did he play? He didn't play anything at all. He was mostly a music director. He'd walk in front of the band with his stick. Remember who was in that band? I can remember. They had a trumpet player. They had Dave Bailey playing drum. Batiste Brown was one of the trumpet players. Now the rest of the musicians, I've just lost memory of them. Is this the band that later became the Gibson band? I think it is. Jackson's band was turned over the Gibson band. That's the band I'm playing with now. E. Gibson's band. And so then after that, let's see, you played with Jackson, was that during the Depression or after? That was after Depression. After Depression, after 1929. That's right. And was it before World War II? It was after World War II. Well how long did you play with Rene? Well Rene, I played with Rene in about a year and a half. That was the first band I started playing with. First time I started playing music. And Perez wasn't as much as it is now. Well who did you work with during the 30s and during World War II? In World War II? No. No. Music wasn't doing much then. I don't think I was playing anybody then. And during the 30s you weren't playing with? No. No. Things was dead then. You didn't get in the WPA band or anything like that? No I didn't get in on that WPA band. I see. So after World War II you joined up with Jackson's band? Yeah. And how long did you stay with Jackson's band? Well I wasn't exactly a steady musician with Jackson. Just whenever he'd be short of a trumpet player he'd use me. I was just an extra there. Don't you have a paper from the union showing when you joined up? Didn't you show me that Sunday? Yeah. Yes I do. Well we could tell from that when you joined the union. I wish I had a... You don't have that with you now? I don't have that with me. If I'd have known this I certainly could have brought it. Well we'll see it later. Yeah. So you don't know about when it was you joined the union? No, no. When I joined the union I was playing with Rene, Kid Rene's band. That's a long time ago. That's right. That's right. Tats' daddy signed that paper you have from the union. It was Tats' daddy, old man Alexander. I think it was. I'm not sure. Yeah that's right. I remember that from Sunday. So after you left Jimmy Jackson who did you go with? Well after I left Jimmy Jackson I wasn't playing any, music was slow then, I wasn't doing much. Now the next band I started playing with was the Eureka. I played with the Eureka quite a while. I guess I overwake myself. I was pressing, I had my own pressing shop, and trying to play music too. Well that caused me to have a nervous breakdown. And I didn't have an idea I'd get strong enough to play music. I had to give all that up, playing music again. And well that's how I did to get out of the union. I was playing with the Eureka when I had that nervous breakdown, not one of those dudes showed up to see anything. What had happened to me? And when I did get up to start back to playing music, my intention was to go back into the union. But I was told he wouldn't permit me that policy. So that's why I had him join back in the union. So he wouldn't give you insurance? He wouldn't give me an insurance policy. All that time I had paid them, had been in there. Well when you were with Jackson, were you in the union? Jackson, no. I don't remember if I paid any union dues when I was with Jackson. Must not have been. I don't remember. I don't think that was a union band. I'm trying to remember. I think it ever was. Plenty how you joined up the Eureka, who were the trumpets in? In the Eureka? Mm-hmm. Poisa Humphrey was one, and T-Boy. T-Boy was the other trumpet player. They had three. Poisa Humphrey, T-Boy and myself. T-Boy and Ramey? Yeah, that's right. He left and went away. And then I think that's when Pagio came in. Well how did that trumpet section work? Who would play the lead when Ramey was there? Well Poisa Humphrey would play the lead. And Ramey would play the second. And I would play second and sometime lead. I didn't have any third parts. Well how would you line up? Who would be on the right? Poisa Humphrey would be on the right. I'd be in the middle. And T-Boy would be on the left side. Well why do they line the trumpets up that way? Who is the middle man? Well your middle man mostly is your second. On your right is your first. And in the middle is your second. Well sometime you get a man to play third but very seldom you get trumpet arranged to that. So it would be two lead men in one second. The second trumpet would be in the middle? Yeah. Well what is the second trumpet part like? What does he play? Well it's mostly, he mostly plays in the staff or under the staff. The second part very seldom would go over the staff. Well does the second trumpet play carry the melody or does he play a harmony part or what? I don't understand. It's mostly a harmony. Or if he has a lead, it's right under the first trumpet part. It's arranged below the first trumpet. And he can hold a lead like that. He'd carry the lead and the other guy would play it up higher the same thing, an octave up. Yeah, that's right. Your second is just an octave lower. Who else was in the Eureka then? Trombones? Well Albert Warner and Sonny Henry, that was the two trombone players. And then as I told you the drummer was, Son was playing drums with him. Son Fuclos. Yeah, he played snare drums. Now I'm trying to think of the bass drummer. I can't call his name. Son Fuclos was a bass drummer. Son was a bass drummer. Not a snare drummer. I can't remember his name. Was he in the band before Arthur Ogle? Hogan you know? No, I don't remember Arthur Ogle. You don't remember him? No. Arthur Ogle and Arthur Ogle. He was a drummer? Mm-hmm, he's a snare drummer. Turn the machine off a second. I don't remember him. I don't remember him. Well, you used to play with him. Yeah. But he was with him for years there. And he lost his legs. He just kind of lost his legs. They had Son White and Ernest Rogers in there too for a while, after him. Yeah. But anyway. I did remember Son White. Mm-hmm. Let's see, when you first came into the Eureka, who was playing tuba? Clok. This man they called Clok. His name is Clok. Red Clok. Yeah, they mostly know him by Red. Did they have baritone horns and pec horns then? No. Or did they have saxophones? No. They had Roddy on sax and Manuel Paul. Two sax. And let me see, who are we missing here? Who haven't we got? Did they have a clarinet ever? Well, sometimes they would use George Lewis. But they mostly used a sax. It's a Roddy and Manuel Paul was a sax player. Very seldom used the clarinet. So as time went on, let's see, who changed in there? Fair little change. Well, this other trumpet player that was playing with Poison Amphrey and myself, I'll call his name just now. Remy, yeah. Well then he left. He went away. And Paggio came in. And that's how things went on. Yeah, I guess they've had too many changes other than that while you were with him. No. Other than Paggio. Things didn't change. No, they didn't. Who was the trumpet player before you were with him? Whose place did you take? I don't, they didn't have, I can't remember any other. You don't remember whose place you took? No, I don't. I know Landry and Schatz were in there for a while. Both of them. Because when I went in there they had T-Boy and Poison Amphrey. Let me see now. So you went in the Eureka. And what did they play? What kind of jobs did they have? Well they mostly played parades. That's all I ever played with them was parades. They have a band for that occasion. Well they had to do something else. They had funerals too. Well that's what I mean. I never did play a dance like with them. Mostly we played with parades. Well they used parades for funerals and these different organizations it turns
out. Were they still having any lawn parties?

No, they're not having. I haven't heard of a lawn party in years. No, I think that would be a good drawing feature if they'd start to give them a few lawn parties. In the summertime, that's because that's out in openings. So the wintertime, this kind of, in the winter season come out, lawn parties just out. It's mostly for the summer. You know, somebody else I wanted to ask you about was Tom Anderson's Place. You mentioned that. Yeah. You said you were down by there, huh? Uh-huh. Did you play in any- Oh you mean in the French Quarters? Yeah. Well in the district, yeah. Yeah. I'm trying to think of a musician that used to be out there. He's a trumpet player. Yeah. Well what did he play like? That's a trumpet player. Yeah, but I mean did he play a lot of high notes or in the staff? Well you see, when you catch the most of trumpet players, like when there's one trumpet in a band, he mostly used, the most he did use was six and seven pieces. Well you take a trumpet player like that, he's even there by himself, he'd play in the staff and over the staff too. Yeah. A long time ago when he'd be fixing to play the ending of a number, he'd mostly go over the staff. He'd play the staff. Oh that's something I wanted to ask you, that reminds me. What special numbers did these trumpet players feature around here? Were there any numbers like say Buddy and Renee, what would they feature? Well they played like the sunny side of the streets. Did they have any real crips? Well they did, but I can't remember the name of them because that was most of their specials, and that was most of the band or the musicians that was playing with them know what they were going to play. They'd say let's play an old number, they'd call any number, probably make the name themselves, and just go on and feature. What did Chris Kelly feature? The trumpet? No I mean tunes. Oh well like I said, Chris would play over the staff, in the staff. Yeah. He was a hot man. But did he play marches or blues or what? Yeah he played both. He was a mixer in music. He played every kind of tune. Yeah he played every kind. I see. Well when you got well and up again and got back in music, who did you join up with? Well I started playing with the E. Gibson band. And I'm playing with them right now. And who's in that band? Well the manager is Spears. And we have another trumpet player, his name is Johnny. John McNeil. John McNeil and Johnny. Oh Johnny, I know. Oh I know, John Wembley. Yeah, yeah that's right. And we have Dave Bailey on bass drums. We have Calvin on trombone. Cal Blunt. Yeah. And we have another trombone player. I can't call his name right now. I'd have to look in my book for his name. Do you have your book with you? No I don't have my book with me. Freddie Miller was there Sunday. Does he play steady with you Freddie? That's him, yeah. He's got Red's trombone. That's him. Yeah, that's Freddie. That's something you know. It's got a five and a half inch bell and it's got a real long bell. It goes away. Chris Balber told me that's a military style trombone. That English trombone player told me that. It is? Says it's a military style, military band. But it gives a nice tone. Yeah it's got a nice tone to it. Let's see, Freddie, Cal, Leon was there on trumpet too Sunday. Yeah. Well in the place of MacNeil, that's who they're using now, Moses, Leon, on trumpet. And we use as Keppert on the bass. Louis Keppert. Louis Keppert. And the snare drummer is who? George Sterling was there. Sterling, that's right. Is he a regular man? Yeah, he's a regular. And Davis on saxophone. What's his first name? I don't know him. On alto. I don't know him. No, I can't call him Davis. Sometimes Lawrence Dent used to play with you. Well, sometimes he'd get in there. Dent plays. He plays clarinet and sax. Let's see, Leon was playing trumpet too sometimes. I'm trying to remember who I've seen through the years with the Gibsons. They had some young kids too from time to time. Eddie Morris too. You know Eddie Morris. Yeah, well that was Eddie Morris. That's an old musician. Yeah, well he used to be with the Gibsons. He played a couple of jobs with the Gibsons. But I don't know what happened. I think Eddie got better jobs. With more study and of course he couldn't be with the Gibsons band then after that happened. Well when you were playing with the Eureka and the Gibsons all through those recent years, did you play any much dance work? No. Since I've been playing with the Gibsons band we played I believe one dance. All the most they do is parades. But you wouldn't go out with other bands and play dances. If I would get an offer I would. But I just, things just sewed up like that. I couldn't get anything else. They're hard. Time to hard.
What kind of job do you like best?

Well I prefer dances. I prefer playing in where people are dancing. Those parades are all right but sometimes you get a job and it looks like they walk all over the city. In Carnival Day you've got to be in condition. You've got to be in condition to walk for Carnival Day. Who did you play for on Carnival Day, what clubs? I think it was the Garden District. I remember the Corner Club used to have some bands too. They'd have those rehearsals first. I used to go up there to the channel and hear those people. Yeah we rehearsed for them too, before they job. This is Sunday before Carnival. That's a lot of fun. It is. I enjoy it. Lots of jobs you get on is work. You're going to feel it at Carnival Day but I am about as much in charge of it. I am about as much enjoyment as Damascus. Yeah. That's fun. Might as well have a good time while you can. Oh yeah, all that makes time pass better. Do you enjoy playing funerals? Well I tell you, a funeral is a funny thing. People that went through that, it brings back memories a little too deep. Of course you can harden up and play them but I don't care too much about funerals. Now after we put the body down, you'll feel a little different. But when you're behind the playing funeral marches, that's plenty deep. I don't care too much about playing funerals. So I don't care too much about playing funerals. But when you're behind the playing funeral marches, that's plenty deep. So I don't care too much about playing funerals. But like these different societies and organizations, that's plenty fun. I could play them every day. I don't care too much about playing funerals. Did you ever remember to play to play to play to play to play to play to play to play to play Did you ever play with the Tuxedo or with George Williams or any of those jump up bands or anything? No, I never did play with the Tuxedo. I tried to, when I first started playing music, trying to learn how to play music, I tried to get in touch with Celestan. He was supposed to help the instrument. But he was so busy, every time I'd go to his house, be my luck to catch him out. So that's why Celestan, he didn't have a chance to show me any music. What I meant with John Casimir. Well that's the Tuxedo band? The Young Tuxedo band? No, I never did play with the Young Tuxedo. You told me something about playing with John and his brother Joe, did you ever play drums? Yeah. With George Jones. You said they were in that band. Yeah, well you see that was like a little make-up band. Like George Jones would get a job out and through the French quarters. He'd come and get John Casimir, Joe Casimir and me and the rest of the men would go and play those jobs. But that wasn't a steady band. Whenever he'd get a job he'd come in the house.
Do you have any questions, Molly?

Not that I can think of right now. Yeah, I thought maybe you had something special on funeral bands or something like that. What are some of the hymns that you all play with the Gibson band? That's one thing I'd like to know. Well the Gibson, they play all those hymns. They play by and by when the morning comes, walk through the streets of the city, over in the glory land, saints. That's about all I can remember. And then they play, they have a march they play. What's the name of that march? We just call the name of that march. Well there's one special march they have, they call it the Gibson March. That's their own make-up. Do they ever play Maryland? Yeah, Maryland. They do play Maryland. That's it. That's about the two marches they play, the Maryland and the E Gibson special. And let's see, do they play any songs, like blues or anything like that ever? Well they play the St. Louis blues, Chic, yeah they play a good many songs. Yeah. Sunny side of the street. Every week. Unless it's a holiday or something happen. Mm-hm. Well we'll get in touch with you if we come. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. That's about all. How often do you rehearse? Well it's every Thursday. Every week. Unless it's a holiday or something happens. Yeah but we could come sometime. I'd be glad to have you there. Well we'll get in touch with you if we come. I'd be glad. Let me see now. What about the Eureka? How often did they rehearse on those times? Well the Eureka would very seldom have rehearsal. Very seldom. What would you do when you wanted to play a new march or something like that? Well that's when they would have rehearsal. See when they'd get a new number they'd call it rehearsal. Otherwise they wouldn't have rehearsal. I guess they knew the stuff pretty well. That's right. They could read pretty good. What about Rene? How often would he have rehearsals if ever? Well Rene would rehearse them. You mean with the Eureka? No Rene. Or Kid Rene. Kid Rene? Kid Rene, not Remy. He would have rehearsals. He'd have rehearsals maybe about three times a month. Yeah he believed in rehearsals. Kid Rene, huh? Yeah. And what would he rehearse you on? Would he rehearse you on the head numbers? Yeah. No music at all. I never knew him to have any music. Mostly head numbers. So you'd work it all out like that, huh? Mm-hmm. Can we stop this just about a minute? Yeah. Yeah, I think we should cut it off nine. .

segments.title: Opening: names and introductions
segments.summary: Richardson and Marjorie Zander give their names to start the recording.

segments.title: Birth, early listening, first teachers and first bands (Hansberry, George Jones, Kid Rena)
segments.summary: Born 1903 in the Battlefield area of New Orleans, he listened to Kid Rena and the Excelsior band, studied with Professor Hansberry and Baptiste Brown, played in George Jones's band, tried his own orchestra, then joined Rena's brass band; also memories of dance halls and Sun Allen and Celestin.

segments.title: Lawn parties, Sam Morgan, and Celestin's trumpet section
segments.summary: Which trumpeters played lawn parties and dances (Buddy Petit, Sam Morgan, Celestin's second trumpets), and that he only played brass band with Rena.

segments.title: Parades and funerals with Kid Rena; watching the Tuxedo band
segments.summary: How seldom Rena's band got parades, the clubs that hired them, how parades looked, and how few funerals they played.

segments.title: Hymns, marches and reading by head in the brass bands
segments.summary: The bands played the same repertoire; hymns for the funeral march out were learned by ear from choir books, while marches such as Maryland were read.

segments.title: Maryland, second-line songs and when the blues were played
segments.summary: Maryland played like the Eureka, return songs for the second line, and blues kept for late dances and slow walking time in the street.

segments.title: Jimmy Jackson's band, the union, and the Eureka brass band
segments.summary: After Rena he played with Jackson's band (later the Gibson band), explains his lack of work in the 1930s and the union dispute after his breakdown, then describes the Eureka's trumpet section and personnel.

segments.title: Trumpet styles, Chris Kelly, and the E. Gibson band personnel
segments.summary: Lawn parties, trumpet playing style and features, then who is in the E. Gibson band now and how little dance work they get.

segments.title: Preferring dances to parades, funerals, and the George Jones make-up band
segments.summary: He prefers dances, finds Carnival Day parades tiring and funerals deeply moving, never played with the Tuxedo, and explains Celestin missing him as a teacher.

segments.title: Gibson band hymns, marches and rehearsal habits; closing
segments.summary: Hymns and the Gibson March played by the Gibson band, weekly Thursday rehearsals versus rare Eureka and frequent Kid Rena rehearsals, then the recording is stopped.
